matches.gold_text: Proposals must be submitted by 2:00 PM ET on October 1, 2025.
The program administrator(s) must develop the curriculum for and administer AI Prep for Track A and/or Track B; ESD will award up to two contracts.
For Track A, the administrator must develop a targeted outreach and recruitment strategy for low-income students.
For Track A, the administrator must provide participant stipends and wrap-around supports including mentorships and career coaches with industry expertise.
The Track A curriculum should consist of online AI courses developed with input from leading researchers and industry experts, with mentorship opportunities and real-world machine learning projects.
For Track B, the administrator must deliver an industry-informed, comprehensive AI technology training program for low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment and connect them to AI jobs.
The Track B program should consist of online AI courses with curriculum that incorporates industry input on technical skills and learning milestones.
The program should serve a minimum of 250 participants, with priority given to applicants that serve more than 400 participants.
Over 50% of program participants should be low-income.
The majority of program graduates should secure paid internships or full-time employment in AI or a closely related field.
Applicants must be organizations with a strong track record in workforce development in AI or similar fields.
If applicants form a team, one organization must be the lead for the proposed programming.

Applicants must have experience in at least three of four domains: academic services to college students, high-tech accelerated training programs, serving low-income populations, and working in the New York market.
Proposed budgets may not exceed $2M for one track or $4M for both tracks over the total contract period, or they will not be considered.
The program operating period funded by ESD is up to 18 months.
Applicants must provide their own budget with associated justification.
Indirect costs are not allowable under this grant and must not be included in the budget.
The extent of any cost matching should be indicated in the budget template.
Awarded applicants must track and record information relevant to the success of the grant, with data points determined during contract negotiation.

The Technical Proposal must include a cover letter describing the organization's mission and history, annual budget, annual number of participants served, employer partnerships, and motivations for applying.
The proposal must describe any work the organization does to train a high-tech workforce in AI and related fields, excluding college students.
The proposal must include a monthly timeline for planning and administering the program through completion of internships or full-time jobs by the first cohort.
The process and timeline should cover curriculum development, recruitment, training duration, cohort size, stipend and supports, and internship or job placement.
The proposal must describe how AI Prep funding will let the organization expand similar existing programming.
The proposal must include one-page resumes of key personnel who would administer the program.
The proposal must include letters from partner employers committing to provide paid internships or full-time employment to graduates.
The proposal must describe how the respondent would define low-income and target recruitment for the applicable Track(s).
The proposal must estimate annual performance on participants served, low-income completion percentage, and placement rate, justified by historical experience or partner commitments.
Respondents should provide a line-by-line price proposal of the proposed fees to accomplish the scope of work.
Respondents must include the Diversity Practices Questionnaire (Appendix B) in their response.
Technical Proposals should be organized with bookmarks matching the information requested in the listed outline.
Respondents should complete and submit the listed Administrative Proposal items in the order listed.
Proposals must be submitted only via the Dropbox upload; facsimile, hardcopy and email submissions will not be accepted.
Respondents must create a main folder named with the company name, RFP title and date of submission.
The main folder must contain two subfolders, one for the Administrative Proposal and one for the Technical Proposal.
Questions about the RFP must be submitted by email, citing the RFP page and section, by the question deadline.
Contractor staff assigned to the project are subject to ESD approval.
The contractor may not subcontract services beyond those indicated in its proposal without prior written approval of the State Project Manager.
ESD sets an overall 30 percent MWBE participation goal, and the contractor must document good faith efforts to use MWBE subcontractors and suppliers.
Respondents must submit an MWBE Utilization Plan with their proposal.

ESD must be named as additional insured on a primary and non-contributory basis on the Commercial General Liability and Auto Liability policies.
For Track A, the administrator must help students secure paid internships.
For Track A, the administrator must create a program application and evaluation process and conduct needs assessments to identify and address student barriers to success.
For Track A, the administrator should propose whether training runs during the academic year or as summer courses, aligned with employer internship hiring cycles.
For Track B, the training schedule should be immersive and deliverable part-time or full-time.
For Track B, the program should provide participant stipends and wrap-around supports, including success coach staff to address barriers to completion.
For Track B, the program should provide full-time job connection support in an AI-related field.
The administrator must cultivate and maintain relationships with leading industry employers, to inform training content and to generate internship or employment opportunities.
Respondents applying for both tracks must describe their organizational capacity and strategy to manage two programs simultaneously.
If a vehicle is used in the business, the selected respondent must carry Commercial Automobile insurance with a limit of at least $1 million.

The contractor must develop the curriculum for and administer the AI Prep program for Track A (AI Prep 4 Internships) and/or Track B (AI Prep 4 Jobs).
Track A (AI Prep 4 Internships) must provide low-income matriculating undergraduate students with AI training aimed at securing paid internship opportunities at leading tech companies.

Track B (AI Prep 4 Jobs) must connect low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment to AI jobs through an accelerated training or bootcamp that serves as an alternative to traditional degree programs.
The administrator must develop and deliver a comprehensive AI technology training program for low-income college students that includes paid internship placements.
The program must create direct pathways from education to the AI industry and help build a talent pipeline for AI employers.
The administrator must develop a targeted outreach and recruitment strategy for low-income students.
The administrator must create a program application and evaluation process.
The administrator must conduct needs assessments to identify and address student barriers to success.
The administrator must design an industry-informed AI curriculum.
The administrator must deliver and manage the AI training program.
The administrator must provide participant stipends and wrap-around supports including mentorships and career coaches with industry expertise.
The administrator must help students secure paid internships.
The administrator must cultivate and maintain relationships with leading industry employers to inform training content and generate paid internship opportunities.
The curriculum must consist of online AI courses developed with input from leading researchers and industry experts, with opportunities for mentorship and real-world machine learning projects.
The proposal must state whether the training program will be offered during the academic year or through summer courses, demonstrating alignment with employer internship hiring cycles and needs.
The training must be tailored to help students secure paid internship placements with leading New York State technology companies.
The internships must allow students to apply their newly acquired AI skills through real-world experience and networking, ultimately leading to full-time jobs.
The program must include a training schedule that is immersive and can be delivered part-time or full-time.
The program must include evaluation metrics to measure participant skill attainment during training.
The program must provide professional development support for trainees throughout training.
The program must state the credentials expected as a result of training completion, if applicable.
The program must provide full-time job connection support in an AI-related field.
ESD will invest up to $2M per track (up to $4M total) to train and provide stipends for participating individuals, capping the award amount.
The award is for an initial term of up to 18 months, with possible renewal or extension based on performance, need, and availability of funds.
An MWBE or SDVOB firm requesting inclusion on the subcontractor interest list must send its contact information and a copy of its NYS MWBE or SDVOB certification to AI.Prep@esd.ny.gov.
The proposed program should serve a minimum of 250 participants.
Proposals that serve more than 400 participants will receive priority.
Over 50% of program participants should be low-income.
The majority of program graduates should secure paid internships or full-time employment in artificial intelligence or a closely related field.
The applicant must be an organization with a strong track record for workforce development in AI or similar fields.
If applicants form a team, one organization must be designated as the lead for the proposed programming.
The applicant must be either a non-profit or a for-profit entity.

The applicant must have experience in at least three of the four listed domains (academic services to college students, high-tech accelerated training programs, serving low-income populations, working in the New York market) to qualify to administer the program.

The vendor must accept that ESD may review all expenses and deny reimbursement of any expenses it deems ineligible.

The proposed budget may include other costs deemed necessary for program success, such as curriculum development and implementation, marketing, and events.
Indirect costs are not an allowable cost under this grant and must not appear in the proposed budget.
Applicants should indicate the extent of cost matching in the budget template.
The awarded applicant must make the tracked data available to ESD upon request.

The awarded applicant must capture and track the data points specified by ESD, with the exact list determined during contract negotiation, including at minimum the number of applicants and the percentage that are low-income.
The awarded applicant must track the number of participants who enroll, including the percentage that are low-income.
The awarded applicant must track the number of participants who complete the program, including the percentage that are low-income.

checklist.fact: The RFP is issued by Empire State Development (ESD) through its Office of Strategic Workforce Development (OSWD), created after Governor Hochul's April 2022 announcement of $350 million for workforce development.

The need is that AI-related jobs often require specialized education and training out of reach for low-income individuals, creating a risk that AI progress will disproportionately benefit those already privileged and leave underrepresented communities behind.

AI Prep is an applied training program with two tracks: Track A (AI Prep 4 Internships) for low-income matriculating undergraduates seeking paid internships, and Track B (AI Prep 4 Jobs) for low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment via accelerated training or bootcamp.
OSWD seeks to award contracts to up to two qualified program administrators to develop the curriculum for and administer AI Prep for Track A and/or Track B.
Funding is up to $2M per track (up to $4M total) for an initial term of up to 18 months, with possible renewal or extension based on performance, need, and availability of funds.
Budgets exceeding $2M for one track or $4M for both tracks over the contract period will not be considered, and indirect costs are not allowable.
Program objectives require serving a minimum of 250 participants (priority for those serving more than 400), with over 50% low-income participants.
Most graduates should secure paid internships or full-time employment in AI or a closely related field.

component_records.title: Program design, curriculum and credential architecture
component_records.description: The bidder delivers an industry-informed AI curriculum built with leading researchers and employer input, covering the applied AI and machine learning content both tracks need, and states the credentials awarded on completion. Curriculum is designed as online AI courses with real-world machine learning projects and mentorship, and is refreshed each cohort against employer demand gathered through the employer-relations workstream. The design fixes cohort size, training duration, part-time and full-time immersive schedules, and the academic-year versus summer delivery pattern so it aligns with employer internship hiring cycles. It also defines the skill-attainment metrics used to measure progress during training and the professional development curriculum delivered alongside technical content.

component_records.title: Track A delivery: AI Prep 4 Internships
component_records.description: For Track A the bidder recruits low-income matriculating undergraduates, runs an application and needs-assessment process, delivers the AI training program, and places students in paid internships at leading New York State technology companies. Each participant receives a stipend plus wrap-around supports — an assigned mentor and a career coach with industry expertise — and internship placements are structured so students apply their AI skills in real-world settings and network toward full-time roles. The track creates a direct pathway from education into the AI industry and builds a talent pipeline for employer partners.

component_records.title: Track B delivery: AI Prep 4 Jobs
component_records.description: For Track B the bidder delivers an accelerated bootcamp alternative to degree programs for low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment, using tailored outreach, an application and assessment process, and part-time or full-time immersive training. Participants receive stipends, success coaches and professional development throughout training, are measured against skill-attainment metrics, and receive full-time AI job connection support through to placement. The track is designed to move participants into AI or closely related roles without a traditional degree.

component_records.title: Employer partnerships and placement engine
component_records.description: The bidder cultivates and maintains relationships with leading industry employers, formalized through partner letters committing to paid internships or full-time jobs, and uses those relationships both to inform curriculum content and to generate placement slots. A placement team matches participants to internships and jobs, coordinates with individual employers on hiring timelines, and tracks placement outcomes by track and low-income status. Employer partners and participating colleges and universities are logged as program data for ESD reporting.

component_records.title: Participant supports, stipends and success services
component_records.description: The bidder administers stipend payments at the proposed per-participant level and delivers wrap-around supports: mentors and career coaches with industry expertise, needs assessments that identify and address barriers to success, and professional development running through training. Support intensity is tiered by assessed need so that participants facing the largest barriers receive the most coaching. Stipend levels and support costs are itemized in the budget so ESD can see how the award is split between training delivery and participant support.

component_records.title: Outreach, recruitment and intake
component_records.description: The bidder runs a targeted outreach and recruitment strategy for low-income participants in both tracks, working through colleges and universities, community nonprofits and New York State workforce channels, and states how it defines low-income for program purposes. Recruitment is sized to the committed participant volume, with a funnel from outreach through application, assessment and enrollment that is tracked at each stage. Intake captures the low-income determination and barrier data needed for later ESD reporting.

component_records.title: Performance measurement, data tracking and ESD reporting
component_records.description: The bidder stands up a participant data system that captures the ESD-specified data points and makes them available to ESD on request: applicant counts and low-income percentages, enrollee counts and low-income percentages, completion counts and low-income percentages, paid internship placement rates and the low-income share of placements, full-time job placement rates and the low-income share, participating colleges and universities, and participating employer partners. The same data produces the annual performance estimates against participants served, low-income completion percentage and placement rate, and supports progress reports and periodic meetings with ESD. Skill-attainment metrics are reported per cohort so ESD can see training effectiveness, not just outcomes.

component_records.title: Budget, pricing and cost governance
component_records.description: The bidder submits a line-by-line price proposal within the $2M per track and $4M combined cap, with Personnel Services costs itemized by job title, named employee, hourly or annual rate, fringe rate, percentage of time and cost to contract, and Other Than Personnel Services costs listed separately with quantities and cost to contract. The budget includes staff salary and benefits, participant stipends and wrap-around supports, and other program costs such as curriculum development, marketing and events, mapped across the 18-month term, with a written justification and any cost match indicated in the budget template. Indirect costs are excluded entirely, and the bidder accepts ESD's right to review all expenses and deny reimbursement of ineligible costs. Change orders are priced at the contract billing rates, and claims for price or time adjustment are asserted within 30 days of ESD's written notification while work continues.

component_records.title: Program governance, staffing and contract compliance
component_records.description: The bidder fields a named program leadership team whose staff are subject to ESD approval, provides a summary of experience and an interview opportunity for any proposed substitute, notifies ESD immediately of staff changes, and aims to keep assigned staff through completion. The bidder accepts the standard Schedule A terms, performs to applicable professional standards, corrects at no charge any services with obvious or patent errors, and accepts that changes are limited to work within the general scope of the contract. The bidder accepts that the contract is not enforceable until OSC review and approval, that proposal costs are borne by the respondent, and that response information may be retained and used by ESD.

component_records.title: Procurement integrity, ethics and insurance compliance
component_records.description: The bidder observes the restricted period by contacting only the designated ESD contacts, makes no gifts to ESD employees, members or directors, and does not discuss employment with ESD staff involved in the procurement within 30 days of the close of their involvement. component_records.title: MWBE, SDVOB and workforce diversity compliance

items.text: The RFP is issued by Empire State Development (ESD), New York State's economic development corporation, whose mission is to promote a growing state economy, encourage business investment and job creation, and support diverse local economies through loans, grants, tax credits, real estate development and marketing.

ESD's Office of Strategic Workforce Development (OSWD) was created under Governor Hochul's April 2022 $350 million workforce development investment and is charged with aligning workforce efforts to employer needs and creating opportunities for unemployed, underemployed and underrepresented workers in the state's highest-growth sectors.

ESD has identified AI as a high-growth sector advancing in healthcare, finance, transportation and manufacturing, with New York positioned as a hub through institutions such as Cornell Tech and state-backed initiatives such as Empire AI.

ESD's stated pain point is that rapid AI advancement may widen economic inequality, because many well-paying AI jobs require specialized education and technical training that low-income individuals cannot access.
ESD also points to tech recruiting practices that favor students at elite schools and those with personal connections to prominent technology companies, which AI Prep is intended to counter.

The procurement is subject to a restricted period under the Procurement Lobbying Law running until contract approval, during which respondents may contact only the designated contacts (Julia Borukhov, primary; Jordan Kaplan, secondary) by email at AI.Prep@esd.ny.gov.

ESD seeks to award contracts to up to two qualified program administrators to develop the curriculum for and administer AI Prep, an applied AI training program with two tracks: Track A "AI Prep 4 Internships" for low-income matriculating undergraduates and Track B "AI Prep 4 Jobs" for low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment.

Track A requires the administrator to recruit low-income college students, run an application and needs-assessment process, deliver an industry-informed online AI curriculum with mentorship and real-world machine learning projects, pay stipends and provide wrap-around supports such as mentors and career coaches, and place students in paid internships with leading New York tech companies.

Track B requires an accelerated training or bootcamp alternative to degree programs, with tailored outreach, online AI courses, an application and assessment process, part-time or full-time immersive training, stipends and success coaches, skill-attainment metrics, professional development, credentials where applicable, and full-time AI job placement support.

ESD will invest up to $2M per track (up to $4M total) to train and stipend participants, for an initial term of up to 18 months with possible renewal or extension based on performance, need and availability of funds.

The program must serve a minimum of 250 participants, with priority for applicants proposing to serve more than 400, and the majority of graduates should secure paid internships or full-time employment in AI or a closely related field.
The anticipated contract start date is January 1, 2026, with the successful respondent announced on November 14, 2025.
Administrators must cultivate and maintain relationships with leading industry employers to inform curriculum content and generate paid internships or full-time jobs for graduates.

Proposals are scored out of a maximum of 100 points by an ESD selection committee, allocated as Firm Qualifications 15 points, Experience 25 points, Project Plan 30 points, Cost of Services 20 points and Diversity Practices 10 points.

The 30-point Project Plan must include a monthly timeline from planning through first-cohort internship or job completion, covering curriculum development, recruitment, training duration, cohort size, stipend level and placement, plus 1-page resumes of key personnel and employer partner letters committing to paid internships or full-time jobs.

Proposers must estimate annual performance against three metrics — total participants served annually, percentage of low-income participants completing the curriculum, and paid internship or full-time job placement rate — justified by historical experience or partner commitments.

The 20-point Cost of Services criterion requires a line-by-line price proposal with PS costs itemized by job title, named employee, hourly or annual rate, fringe rate, percentage of time and cost to contract, and OTPS costs listed separately with quantities.
The 10-point Diversity Practices score is awarded by ESD's Office of Contractor and Supplier Diversity based on the Appendix B Diversity Practices Questionnaire submitted with the response.

Questions must be submitted by email to AI.Prep@esd.ny.gov citing RFP page and section by August 29, 2025, with ESD responses due September 12, 2025, and proposals are due by 2:00 PM ET on October 1, 2025, with late proposals not accepted.
ESD reserves the right to conduct reference checks at its sole discretion and to use reference information in evaluating proposals.
Budgets exceeding $2M for one track or $4M for both tracks over the total contract period will not be considered, and indirect costs are not an allowable expense.

Applicants must be non-profit or for-profit entities with experience in at least three of four domains: academic services to college students, high-tech accelerated training programs, serving low-income populations, and working in the New York market; teams are allowed but one organization must be the lead.
There is no cost-match requirement, but cost-matching earns additional points in scoring and must be indicated in the budget template.

Awarded administrators must track and report ESD-specified data, including applicant and enrollee counts and low-income percentages, completion rates, internship and job placement rates, and participating colleges and employer partners, with the exact list set during contract negotiation.

The contract carries a 30% MWBE participation goal and a 6% SDVOB participation goal, requiring an MWBE Utilization Plan and an SDVOB Utilization Plan on Form OCSD-4 with the proposal and quarterly and monthly compliance reporting thereafter.

The selected respondent must carry Commercial General Liability of $1M per occurrence and $2M aggregate, Commercial Auto of $1M if a vehicle is used, Sexual Abuse and Molestation insurance of $1M, statutory Workers' Compensation/Employer's Liability and Disability coverage, naming ESD as additional insured on a primary and non-contributory basis with waivers of subrogation.

Proposals must be uploaded as a two-part submission (separate Administrative and Technical Proposal subfolders inside a folder named "company name – RFP title – date of Submission") to the Dropbox at https://www.dropbox.com/request/AIPrep; fax, hardcopy and email submissions are not accepted.

Appendix A (ESD IT Security Standard Brief) and Appendix B (Diversity Practices Questionnaire) are referenced as separate documents, and a sample Schedule A of standard contract terms is referenced by link; bidders must obtain these and submit any Schedule A concerns in writing with the Administrative Proposal or waive objections.
ESD's anticipated contract start date is January 1, 2026, so curriculum build must be compressed into the first months of the term.
Track A is aimed at low-income matriculating undergraduates and requires paid internship placements with leading New York tech companies.
Track B must serve low-income New Yorkers with barriers to employment through an accelerated training or bootcamp alternative to degree programs.
Administrators must cultivate and maintain employer relationships that inform curriculum and generate paid internships or full-time jobs.
ESD will invest up to $2M per track to train and stipend participants, so stipend levels must be set within that cap.
The program must serve a minimum of 250 participants, with priority for proposals serving more than 400.
The exact list of tracked data points is set during contract negotiation, with applicant and enrollee counts and low-income percentages required at minimum.
Budgets exceeding $2M for one track or $4M for both tracks will not be considered, and indirect costs are not allowable.
The award is for an initial term of up to 18 months with possible renewal or extension based on performance, need and availability of funds.
The procurement is subject to a restricted period under the Procurement Lobbying Law running until contract approval, with contact limited to the designated contacts by email.
The contract carries a 30% MWBE participation goal and a 6% SDVOB participation goal, with quarterly and monthly compliance reporting thereafter.
Questions are due August 29, 2025, ESD answers are due September 12, 2025, and proposals are due October 1, 2025 at 2:00 PM ET.
The bidder proposes on both tracks as a single lead organization, with the $4M combined cap applying and a documented capacity plan for running two programs simultaneously.
The bidder adopts its own published low-income definition and barrier criteria, stated explicitly in the proposal, and applies them consistently to recruitment and to all low-income reporting.
The program is sized at more than 400 participants across both tracks to earn priority scoring, with cohort size and internship duration set by the bidder and stated in the monthly timeline.
Stipends and wrap-around supports are funded from the award rather than by employers, with the stipend level proposed by the bidder and itemized in the budget.
The budget is phased across the 18-month initial term only, with any renewal priced separately and not assumed in the proposal.
The bidder prices to the full $2M per track ceiling and treats all costs other than indirect costs as eligible unless ESD rules otherwise at review.
The bidder submits pricing in its own line-by-line format following the PS and OTPS breakdown in the RFP, since no prescribed cost workbook is provided.
Cost figures are placed in the Cost of Services section of the Technical Proposal as the RFP's structure requires, and no other pricing appears elsewhere in the technical volume.
The bidder assumes OSC review and approval will be required and plans mobilization so that no billable work begins before approval.
The bidder assumes the full insurance schedule applies, including Commercial Auto, Sexual Abuse and Molestation coverage and waivers of subrogation, and prices the premiums accordingly.
The bidder treats the 30% MWBE and 6% SDVOB goals as commitments backed by named subcontractors in the Utilization Plans, with good faith effort evidence assembled in case a waiver is needed.
The bidder assumes the Workforce Utilization Report and monthly SDVOB compliance reporting formats will be issued by ESD after award and builds a reporting capability flexible enough to absorb them.
The bidder assumes the data-point list will be finalized at contract negotiation and proposes the minimum set in the RFP plus a small buffer of related fields.

The bidder assumes the Appendix A IT Security Standard Brief applies to participant and program data and will meet it through its data system design, obtaining the brief before finalizing the technical approach.

The bidder assumes the Appendix B Diversity Practices Questionnaire and the OCSD, Schedule A and tax forms will be obtained from the links in the RFP and completed before the October 1, 2025 deadline.
The bidder assumes the stated question and proposal deadlines are firm despite ESD's right to change dates, and plans its submission accordingly.
The bidder assumes Schedule A concerns must be raised in writing with the Administrative Proposal and raises none, accepting Schedule A as offered.

Schedule A contract terms unavailable before the bid. The standard contract terms the successful respondent must accept are referenced only by link and are not in the RFP, yet objections must be raised in writing with the Administrative Proposal or are waived. The bidder is therefore pricing and committing to an unseen contract, and any unacceptable term (liability, indemnity, IP, termination) discovered after award becomes rework or a dispute. The proposed solution assumes Schedule A is acceptable and raises no concerns. Schedule A is a mandatory acceptance item (R115, R260) and the RFP waives objections not raised with the Administrative Proposal, so silence is a binding choice made without the text.

Appendix A IT security standard unseen while data system is designed. Appendix A, the ESD IT Security Standard Brief, is referenced but not included, so the security controls the participant data system must meet are unknown. If the standard requires controls the proposed design does not include (encryption, hosting location, access logging, incident reporting), the data system needs rework after award, inside a compressed mobilization window. The solution assumes the brief applies and will be obtained before the technical approach is final. The solution commits to a participant data system and to meeting Appendix A, but the standard's content is not in the RFP; rework would land in months 1-3 of an 18-month term.

Budget cap may not cover 400+ participants with stipends and supports. The award is capped at $2M per track and $4M combined for an 18-month term, and the same money must fund curriculum, staff, stipends, wrap-around supports, employer relations and reporting. The solution sizes the program above 400 participants to earn priority scoring and prices to the full ceiling, so any underestimate of stipend or support cost per participant has no headroom and cannot be recovered through indirect costs, which are barred. The per-participant cost figures are the bidder's assumption, not figures the RFP supplies. The cap is a hard disqualifier and indirect costs are unallowable, while the solution simultaneously maximizes participant volume and stipend commitments within that cap.

Compressed mobilization against a January 1, 2026 start. Award is announced November 14, 2025 and the anticipated start is January 1, 2026, with OSC review and approval required before the contract is enforceable. The solution compresses curriculum build, employer commitments and recruitment into months 1-3, so any delay in OSC approval or in hiring named staff pushes first-cohort intake and the placement timeline. The bidder bears proposal costs and cannot bill before approval. The solution's own design puts curriculum and employer build in the first quarter of an 18-month term, and the RFP makes the contract unenforceable until OSC approves.

Employer partner letters and placement commitments are the scoring and delivery hinge. The Project Plan requires employer letters committing to paid internships or full-time jobs, and the outcome metrics depend on those placements. The solution relies on a placement engine and partner letters but the RFP does not guarantee employer demand, and the bidder must estimate placement rates from historical experience or partner commitments. If letters are thin or placements fall short, both the 30-point Project Plan and the contractual performance assessment suffer. Placement rate is a reported metric and a scored estimate, and the solution's delivery model depends on employer commitments that are outside the bidder's control.

MWBE 30% and SDVOB 6% goals carry liquidated damages and payment withholding. The contract sets a 30% MWBE and 6% SDVOB participation goal, requires Utilization Plans with the proposal, monthly SDVOB reporting by the 10th and quarterly Workforce Utilization Reports, and makes willful failure a breach with liquidated damages equal to the shortfall. The solution commits to named subcontractors and treats the goals as commitments; if certified firms cannot be found for the scope, the bidder faces damages, withheld payment or a waiver fight. The availability of certified firms for AI training work is an assumption, not a fact the RFP supplies. The goals are backed by liquidated damages and payment withholding, and the solution converts them into firm commitments before certified subcontractors are confirmed.

Appendix B Diversity Practices Questionnaire missing from a 10-point criterion. The Diversity Practices Questionnaire that ESD's Office of Contractor and Supplier Diversity scores for 10 of 100 points is referenced but not provided. Without the form the bidder cannot see what practices are scored, and submitting an incomplete or improvised questionnaire risks losing points the proposal cannot recover elsewhere. The solution assumes the form will be obtained from the RFP links before the October 1 deadline. Ten points of a 100-point score depend on a form that is not in the RFP, and the solution only assumes it will be retrieved.

Undefined low-income and barrier criteria drive recruitment and reporting. The RFP does not define 'low-income' or 'barriers to employment', yet the program must serve a majority low-income participants and report low-income percentages for applicants, enrollees, completers and placements. The solution adopts its own definition; if ESD applies a different threshold at contract negotiation, recruitment targets, eligibility screening and every reported percentage must be redone. The same applies to the data-point list, which is only fixed at negotiation. The solution explicitly assumes its own definition will be accepted, and the RFP leaves both the definition and the data-point list open until negotiation.

Schedule A / ST-220 conflict on sub-consultant tax information. One requirement says Schedule A to Form ST 220-TD must carry detailed sub-consultant information such as tax ID numbers, while another forbids including Schedule A information in the proposal submission. A bidder using subcontractors for MWBE/SDVOB participation cannot tell where that information belongs, and a misplaced or omitted submission can render the proposal non-responsive. The solution assumes Schedule A concerns are raised in writing and raises none. The two requirements directly contradict each other and the ST-220-CA is a pass/fail responsiveness item; the solution does not resolve the conflict.

Technical volume scope conflict: everything requested versus nothing extra. The RFP asks for a proposal that provides all requested information clearly and concisely, and separately forbids any information beyond what is specifically requested. A bidder that adds context, marketing material or cross-references to strengthen the 30-point Project Plan risks a compliance deduction, while a minimal response risks losing content points. The solution places cost figures in the Technical Proposal's Cost of Services section, which sits close to this line. The two requirements are in direct tension and the RFP scores conformance and completeness; the solution's choice to put pricing in the technical volume is an interpretation, not a settled rule.

Insurance schedule priced blind, including Sexual Abuse and Molestation cover. The RFP requires Commercial General Liability, Commercial Auto where a vehicle is used, $1M Sexual Abuse and Molestation coverage, Workers' Compensation, Disability, additional-insured status and waivers of subrogation, but qualifies the list as 'at a minimum and to the extent applicable'. The solution assumes the full schedule applies and prices the premiums; if a coverage is not actually required the bid is overpriced, and if an unlisted coverage is required the cost is unbudgeted inside a capped award. The applicability qualifier leaves the mandatory set unsettled, and the solution resolves it by assuming the maximum, which is a pricing assumption rather than a confirmed requirement.

Two-track delivery with one lead organization and undisclosed subcontracting limits. The solution bids both tracks as a single lead organization with a shared curriculum and employer engine, and the RFP requires a detailed capacity plan for running two programs simultaneously. Subcontracting is only permitted if indicated in the proposal or approved in writing later, and staff changes require ESD approval with an interview for each substitute. If the capacity plan is unconvincing the proposal loses Project Plan points; if delivery strains, the bidder cannot freely add subcontractors or swap staff. The solution takes on both tracks and relies on subcontractors for MWBE/SDVOB participation, while the RFP restricts undisclosed subcontracting and staff substitution.
